```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r library}
library(rmet)
x <- rmet_example
```

Hourly INMET data look simple, but three conventions decide whether daily
values computed from them are right: how the hours are stamped, which day an
hour belongs to, and what to do with missing hours. This vignette explains each
one and how `inmet_daily()` handles it.

## 1. Timestamps are UTC and mark the end of the hour

The historical files record time in UTC. `inmet_read()` keeps it that way by
default, so `datetime` is unambiguous for every station in the country:

```{r utc}
x$datetime[1:3]
attr(x$datetime, "tzone")
```

Many columns describe the hour that *ends* at the timestamp: precipitation is
the total of the previous hour, and `temp_max_prev_c` and `temp_min_prev_c` are
the highest and lowest air temperature during that hour. The record stamped
`03:00 UTC` therefore covers 02:00 to 03:00 UTC, which is 23:00 to midnight in
Porto Alegre.

Displaying the same instants in local time only changes how they print:

```{r local}
local <- x$datetime[1:3]
attr(local, "tzone") <- "America/Sao_Paulo"
local
```

## 2. Which day does an hour belong to?

A daily maximum in Brazil should be the maximum of a *local* day. Grouping by
`as.Date(datetime)` uses UTC days instead, which in Porto Alegre run from
21:00 to 21:00 local time (22:00 to 22:00 during daylight saving time, which
Brazil observed until 2019). An evening shower or a hot late afternoon can then
land on the wrong day.

`inmet_daily()` assigns each record to the local day containing the middle of
its hour (`datetime` minus 30 minutes). The two choices give different days:

```{r compare-days}
utc_day <- as.Date(x$datetime)
local_day <- as.Date(x$datetime - 1800, tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")
mean(utc_day != local_day)
```

One hour in six (the records stamped 00:00 to 03:00 UTC) is placed on a
different day, and the differences matter for daily totals and extremes:

```{r compare-values}
wrong <- tapply(x$precip_mm, utc_day, sum)
right <- inmet_daily(x, min_hours = 1)
right <- setNames(right$precip_mm, right$date)
common <- intersect(names(wrong), names(right))
summary(abs(wrong[common] - right[common]))
```

For stations in other time zones (for example Amazonas, Acre, or Mato Grosso)
pass the local zone explicitly, such as `tz = "America/Manaus"`. Use
`tz = "UTC"` when you want UTC days on purpose.

## 3. Missing hours

INMET files contain rows for every hour of the year, including hours when a
station was not reporting. By default `inmet_read()` drops rows in which *every*
measurement is missing (`drop_empty = FALSE` keeps them). Individual variables
can still be missing in the rows that remain.

A daily total over a day with half its hours missing is not a daily total.
`inmet_daily()` therefore computes a variable only when it has at least
`min_hours` valid hourly values that day (20 by default), and reports the
number of hourly records in `n_hours`:

```{r completeness}
daily <- inmet_daily(x)
table(cut(daily$n_hours, c(0, 12, 19, 23, 25), right = TRUE))
daily[daily$n_hours < 20, c("date", "n_hours", "temp_max_c", "precip_mm")]
```

Choose `min_hours` to suit the variable and the analysis: precipitation totals
are sensitive to every missing hour, while a daily maximum of temperature is
usually reached in the afternoon. Radiation is an exception: it is missing at
night at most stations, so `radiation_mj_m2` sums whatever daytime values are
present (see `?inmet_daily`).

## 4. Which temperature columns?

The hourly files contain both the air temperature at the top of the hour
(`temp_dry_c`) and its extremes during the previous hour
(`temp_max_prev_c`, `temp_min_prev_c`). The daily maximum and minimum should
come from the extremes; the instantaneous values miss the peaks between
readings:

```{r extremes}
from_extremes <- inmet_daily(x)$temp_max_c
from_hourly <- inmet_daily(x[, setdiff(names(x), "temp_max_prev_c")])$temp_max_c
summary(from_extremes - from_hourly)
```

At Porto Alegre in 2023 the hourly readings underestimate the daily maximum by
about half a degree on average, and by more than two degrees on some days.

`inmet_daily()` uses the extremes when they are present and falls back to
`temp_dry_c` otherwise.

## 5. Quality control is up to you

INMET labels automatic-station observations as raw data. Before relying on
daily values, check for impossible values, flat-lining sensors, and sudden
jumps, for example:

```{r qc}
summary(x$temp_dry_c)
sum(x$temp_max_prev_c < x$temp_min_prev_c, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Comparing with nearby stations (`inmet_nearest()`) is often the most effective
check for isolated errors.
